text: What is Docker primarily used for?
choices: Packaging and running applications in containers
explanation:
Packaging and running applications in containers is correct because Docker packages an application with its dependencies so it can run consistently across environments.

Example: a Node.js API and its runtime can be shipped together in one container image.

text: What is a Docker image?
choices: A read-only template used to create containers
A running process with mutable state
explanation:
A read-only template used to create containers is correct because an image contains the filesystem, runtime, and metadata needed to start containers.

Example: an image can include an app JAR, a JRE, and an entrypoint command.

text: What is a Docker container?
choices: A running instance of a Docker image
explanation:
A running instance of a Docker image is correct because containers are started from images and run as isolated processes on the host.

Example: starting two containers from the same image creates two separate running instances.

text: Which file is commonly used to define how a Docker image is built?
explanation:
Dockerfile is correct because a Dockerfile describes the steps and instructions Docker uses to assemble an image.

Example: it can copy application files and declare the command used at startup.

text: Which command is commonly used to build an image from a Dockerfile?
explanation:
docker build is correct because the build command reads the Dockerfile and creates an image layer by layer.

Example: docker build -t quiz-app .

text: Which command starts a new container from an image?
explanation:
docker run is correct because the run command creates and starts a container from a selected image.

Example: docker run -p 8080:8080 quiz-app

text: What does a Dockerfile FROM instruction do?
explanation:
Specifies the base image is correct because FROM sets the starting point for the image by choosing an existing base image.

Example: FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre

text: What does the COPY instruction do in a Dockerfile?
choices: Copies files from the build context into the image
explanation:
Copies files from the build context into the image is correct because COPY is used to place application files, configs, or artifacts into the image filesystem.

Example: COPY target/app.jar /app/app.jar

text: What does the RUN instruction do in a Dockerfile?
choices: Executes a command during image build
Runs only when the container starts
explanation:
Executes a command during image build is correct because RUN is used for build-time steps like installing packages or preparing files.

Example: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl

text: What does the CMD instruction usually define?
choices: The default command for the container at startup
explanation:
The default command for the container at startup is correct because CMD provides the default runtime command if none is overridden when the container starts.

Example: CMD ["node", "server.js"]

text: What is the difference between CMD and RUN?
choices: RUN executes at build time while CMD provides the default runtime command
CMD creates images while RUN creates networks
RUN is only for Windows containers
explanation:
RUN executes at build time while CMD provides the default runtime command is correct because they serve different phases: image creation versus container startup behavior.

Example: install dependencies with RUN, then start the app with CMD.

text: What does ENTRYPOINT usually define?
choices: The main executable for the container
explanation:
The main executable for the container is correct because ENTRYPOINT fixes the executable so the container behaves like a dedicated command.

Example: ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]

text: Which instruction documents a port the container listens on?
explanation:
EXPOSE is correct because EXPOSE records the intended container port for documentation and tooling purposes.

Example: EXPOSE 8080

text: Does EXPOSE publish a port to the host by itself?
choices: No, it only documents the container port
Yes, it automatically opens the firewall
explanation:
No, it only documents the container port is correct because port publishing happens at runtime with options like -p, not from EXPOSE alone.

Example: you still need docker run -p 8080:8080 ....

text: Which flag publishes a container port to the host?
explanation:
-p is correct because the -p flag maps a host port to a container port so external clients can reach the service.

Example: -p 4200:80 maps host port 4200 to container port 80.

text: What does the -d flag do with docker run?
choices: Runs the container in detached mode
explanation:
Runs the container in detached mode is correct because detached mode starts the container in the background instead of attaching to the terminal.

Example: docker run -d nginx

text: Which command shows running containers?
explanation:
docker ps is correct because docker ps lists the containers currently running on the host.

Example: it shows container IDs, image names, and published ports.

text: Which command shows all containers including stopped ones?
explanation:
docker ps -a is correct because adding -a includes exited containers as well as running ones.

Example: useful when checking why a container exited unexpectedly.

text: Which command lists locally available images?
explanation:
docker images is correct because docker images shows repositories, tags, and image sizes stored on the machine.

Example: it helps confirm whether quiz-app:latest exists locally.

text: Which command removes a stopped container?
explanation:
docker rm is correct because docker rm deletes container metadata after the container has stopped.

Example: remove a test container after it exits to keep the host tidy.

text: Which command stops a running container gracefully?
explanation:
docker stop is correct because docker stop sends a termination signal and then forces shutdown only if needed after a timeout.

Example: stop a web server container before replacing it with a new version.

text: Which command forcibly terminates a running container immediately?
explanation:
docker kill is correct because docker kill sends a stronger signal immediately and is usually less graceful than docker stop.

Example: use it when a container ignores normal shutdown.

text: Which command displays logs from a container?
explanation:
docker logs is correct because docker logs shows stdout and stderr output produced by the container process.

Example: checking logs can reveal startup errors or stack traces.

text: Which command allows you to execute a command inside a running container?
explanation:
docker exec is correct because docker exec runs an additional command inside an already running container.

Example: docker exec -it app sh

text: What does the -it combination commonly mean with docker exec or docker run?
explanation:
Interactive terminal mode is correct because the combination allocates a pseudo-terminal and keeps stdin open for interactive use.

Example: it is commonly used to open a shell inside a container.

text: Which command shows detailed low-level information about a container or image?
explanation:
docker inspect is correct because docker inspect returns structured metadata such as network settings, mounts, and configuration.

Example: it can show the container IP address or entrypoint configuration.

text: Which command shows the processes running inside a container?
explanation:
docker top is correct because docker top displays the process list for a given container.

Example: useful when confirming which command is actually running as PID 1.

text: Which command shows resource usage of running containers?
explanation:
docker stats is correct because docker stats streams CPU, memory, and network metrics for active containers.

Example: it helps identify a container using unusually high memory.

text: What is a Docker volume primarily used for?
choices: Persisting data outside a container writable layer
explanation:
Persisting data outside a container writable layer is correct because volumes let data survive container replacement and are the usual storage mechanism for persistent container data.

Example: a database container stores data in a volume so records remain after restart.

text: Which flag mounts a volume or bind mount into a container?
explanation:
-v is correct because the -v flag attaches storage from the host or a named volume into the container filesystem.

Example: -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data

text: What is a bind mount?
choices: A direct mount of a host path into the container
A volume stored only in the registry
explanation:
A direct mount of a host path into the container is correct because bind mounts use an existing host directory or file instead of a Docker-managed volume.

Example: mount local source code into a container during development.

text: When is a bind mount commonly useful?
choices: During local development when container code should reflect host file changes
explanation:
During local development when container code should reflect host file changes is correct because bind mounts are handy when developers want live file edits from the host to be visible in the container.

Example: a frontend dev server container reads source files from the local project folder.

text: What is a named volume?
choices: A Docker-managed persistent storage volume with a reusable name
A read-only snapshot of a container
explanation:
A Docker-managed persistent storage volume with a reusable name is correct because named volumes are managed by Docker and can be attached to multiple containers when needed.

Example: a MySQL container can use a named volume called mysql-data.

text: Which command lists Docker volumes?
explanation:
docker volume ls is correct because the volume subcommand helps inspect storage objects managed by Docker.

Example: use it to confirm whether a named volume exists before attaching it.

text: Which command removes unused volumes?
explanation:
docker volume prune is correct because pruning helps reclaim disk space by deleting dangling volumes that are no longer in use.

Example: useful after many test runs create abandoned volumes.

text: What is a Docker network?
choices: A virtual network that connects containers and optionally the host
explanation:
A virtual network that connects containers and optionally the host is correct because Docker networks allow containers to communicate using isolated or shared network configurations.

Example: a web container and a database container can talk over the same user-defined bridge network.

text: Which default network type do standalone containers often use if none is specified?
explanation:
bridge is correct because the bridge network is the common default for local single-host Docker usage.

Example: a container started with no custom network joins the default bridge network.

text: What does the host network mode generally do?
choices: Shares the host network stack with the container
explanation:
Shares the host network stack with the container is correct because host networking removes network namespace isolation so the container uses host ports directly.

Example: this can reduce overhead but sacrifices normal port mapping isolation.

text: What does the none network mode do?
choices: Routes traffic through the host by default
explanation:
Disables container networking is correct because none mode starts the container without network interfaces other than loopback.

Example: useful for tightly controlled offline batch workloads.

text: Which command creates a user-defined network?
explanation:
docker network create is correct because user-defined networks make service-to-service communication easier and often provide built-in DNS resolution.

Example: create one network for an app container and its database.

text: Why are user-defined bridge networks often preferred over the default bridge?
choices: They provide better isolation and built-in name resolution between containers
They remove the need for images
explanation:
They provide better isolation and built-in name resolution between containers is correct because custom bridge networks are easier to manage for multi-container apps and support container-name DNS.

Example: the API container can reach the database at db instead of using an IP address.

text: What is Docker Compose commonly used for?
explanation:
Defining and running multi-container applications is correct because Compose lets developers declare services, networks, volumes, and environment variables in one file.

Example: a web app, API, and database can be started together from one configuration.

text: Which file name is commonly associated with Docker Compose?
explanation:
docker-compose.yml or compose.yml is correct because Compose reads service definitions from a YAML file with one of the standard compose file names.

Example: a project root may contain compose.yml listing app and database services.

text: Which command starts services defined in a Compose file?
explanation:
docker compose up is correct because the up command creates and starts the services declared in the Compose configuration.

Example: docker compose up -d starts the full app in detached mode.

text: Which command stops and removes services started by Docker Compose?
explanation:
docker compose down is correct because the down command tears down containers, networks, and optionally related resources from a Compose app.

Example: use it after local testing is finished.

text: Where are environment variables commonly declared for a Compose service?
choices: Under the environment section or in an env file
explanation:
Under the environment section or in an env file is correct because Compose supports service-specific environment variables directly in YAML or indirectly through env files.

Example: a database password can come from a .env file during local development.

text: What does docker compose logs show?
choices: Logs from one or more Compose-managed services
explanation:
Logs from one or more Compose-managed services is correct because Compose logs helps inspect output across a multi-service application defined in the compose file.

Example: see both API and database logs while troubleshooting startup issues.

text: What is a multi-stage Docker build?
choices: A build that uses multiple FROM stages to reduce final image size and separate build tools from runtime
A build that can only run on multiple hosts
A way to merge two registries
explanation:
A build that uses multiple FROM stages to reduce final image size and separate build tools from runtime is correct because multi-stage builds keep the final image lean by copying only needed artifacts from earlier build stages.

Example: compile a Java app in one stage and copy only the JAR into a minimal runtime stage.

text: Why are multi-stage builds useful?
choices: They reduce final image size and attack surface
They remove the need for tagging
explanation:
They reduce final image size and attack surface is correct because smaller runtime images are often faster to pull and include fewer unnecessary tools or dependencies.

Example: the final image does not need Maven if Maven was only used in the build stage.

text: What is an image tag?
choices: A label that identifies a specific image version
explanation:
A label that identifies a specific image version is correct because tags help distinguish image variants such as versions, environments, or release candidates.

Example: my-app:1.4.0 and my-app:latest are different tags.

text: Which command adds another tag to an existing image?
explanation:
docker tag is correct because docker tag creates another name reference pointing to the same local image ID.

Example: tag a locally built image before pushing it to a registry namespace.

text: What is Docker Hub?
choices: A container runtime inside Linux kernels
explanation:
A public container image registry is correct because Docker Hub stores and distributes container images that can be pulled by name and tag.

Example: many official base images like nginx or python are hosted there.

text: Which command downloads an image from a registry?
explanation:
docker pull is correct because pull retrieves an image and its layers from a configured registry.

Example: docker pull postgres:16

text: Which command uploads an image to a registry?
explanation:
docker push is correct because push sends a tagged local image to a remote registry so other hosts can pull it.

Example: push a CI-built image to Docker Hub or a private registry.

text: What is a container registry?
choices: A service that stores and distributes container images
explanation:
A service that stores and distributes container images is correct because registries are the main distribution mechanism for container images across environments.

Example: Docker Hub, Amazon ECR, and GitHub Container Registry are all registries.

text: Why should container images usually be versioned with explicit tags in production?
choices: To make deployments reproducible and avoid ambiguity
Because containers cannot be rolled back
explanation:
To make deployments reproducible and avoid ambiguity is correct because explicit version tags help teams know exactly what was deployed and make rollback easier.

Example: deploy api:2.3.1 instead of relying only on latest.

text: Why is relying only on the latest tag risky?
choices: Its meaning can change over time and make deployments unpredictable
explanation:
Its meaning can change over time and make deployments unpredictable is correct because latest is just another mutable tag, so it may point to different image content at different times.

Example: two environments may both use latest but actually run different builds.

text: What does docker history show?
choices: The layer history of an image
Only running processes in a container
explanation:
The layer history of an image is correct because history reveals how an image was built and can highlight unexpectedly large layers.

Example: it helps diagnose why an image size increased after a Dockerfile change.

text: What does .dockerignore do?
choices: Excludes files from the build context sent to Docker
Ignores image tags in a registry
explanation:
Excludes files from the build context sent to Docker is correct because .dockerignore reduces build context size and avoids copying unnecessary or sensitive files into builds.

Example: exclude node_modules, target, or local secrets.

text: Why is .dockerignore important?
choices: It makes builds faster and avoids sending unnecessary files
It publishes ports at build time
explanation:
It makes builds faster and avoids sending unnecessary files is correct because smaller build contexts improve performance and reduce accidental leakage of local artifacts into the image build.

Example: do not send a huge .git folder to every build unless needed.

text: What is the Docker build context?
choices: The set of files sent to the Docker daemon for a build
explanation:
The set of files sent to the Docker daemon for a build is correct because Docker builds operate on the provided context, usually the current directory, rather than arbitrary host paths.

Example: docker build . uses the current folder as the context.

text: Why is keeping images small generally beneficial?
choices: Smaller images are faster to transfer and often have fewer unnecessary components
They cannot run out of memory
They remove the need for logs
explanation:
Smaller images are faster to transfer and often have fewer unnecessary components is correct because lean images improve pull times and can reduce attack surface by containing fewer packages.

Example: using a slim runtime image usually deploys faster than a full build environment image.

text: What is a common reason to avoid running containers as root?
choices: It reduces security risk if the container is compromised
explanation:
It reduces security risk if the container is compromised is correct because least-privilege practices help limit what an attacker can do if they escape or exploit the application.

Example: create a non-root user in the image before starting the app process.

text: Which Dockerfile instruction changes the active user for subsequent instructions and runtime?
explanation:
USER is correct because USER sets which Linux user the following instructions and default container process should run as.

Example: USER appuser

text: What does the WORKDIR instruction do?
choices: Sets the working directory for subsequent Dockerfile instructions
Publishes the current folder as a volume
explanation:
Sets the working directory for subsequent Dockerfile instructions is correct because WORKDIR avoids repeating long paths and affects where commands run and files are copied relative to.

Example: WORKDIR /app

text: Which Dockerfile instruction sets environment variables in the image?
explanation:
ENV is correct because ENV defines environment variables available during later build steps and at runtime unless overridden.

Example: ENV NODE_ENV=production

text: What is the difference between ARG and ENV?
choices: ARG is for build-time variables while ENV persists into the image runtime environment
explanation:
ARG is for build-time variables while ENV persists into the image runtime environment is correct because ARG is typically used during build, while ENV remains in the image and affects container runtime behavior.

Example: use ARG for a build version and ENV for application configuration defaults.

text: Should secrets usually be stored directly in a Dockerfile with ENV?
choices: No, secrets should generally be provided through safer runtime or build mechanisms
Yes, that is the preferred secure method
explanation:
No, secrets should generally be provided through safer runtime or build mechanisms is correct because baking secrets into images can leak them through image history, registries, or shared environments.

Example: database passwords should come from secret managers or runtime environment injection.

text: What is container immutability in practice?
choices: Treating containers as disposable and replacing them instead of modifying them in place
Preventing any writes inside a process
explanation:
Treating containers as disposable and replacing them instead of modifying them in place is correct because immutable infrastructure practices make deployments more predictable because changes come from rebuilt images, not manual edits.

Example: rebuild and redeploy a fixed image instead of patching files inside a live container.

text: Why is docker exec into production containers usually discouraged for routine changes?
choices: Manual in-container changes are hard to track and are lost when containers are replaced
explanation:
Manual in-container changes are hard to track and are lost when containers are replaced is correct because operational changes should generally come from source-controlled image builds and deployments.

Example: update app config via a new deployment rather than editing files interactively in a running container.

text: What is the purpose of a health check in Docker?
choices: To let Docker determine whether a container is functioning properly
explanation:
To let Docker determine whether a container is functioning properly is correct because health checks provide a way to monitor application readiness beyond simply seeing that the process is running.

Example: an HTTP endpoint can be checked periodically to verify the app still responds.

text: Which Dockerfile instruction defines a container health check?
explanation:
HEALTHCHECK is correct because HEALTHCHECK declares the command Docker should run to test whether the container is healthy.

Example: HEALTHCHECK CMD curl -f http://localhost:8080/health || exit 1

text: What is the purpose of docker system prune?
choices: To remove unused Docker data such as stopped containers and dangling images
explanation:
To remove unused Docker data such as stopped containers and dangling images is correct because pruning helps reclaim disk space after lots of builds and test containers accumulate.

Example: it can delete old stopped containers and unused networks.

text: What is a dangling image?
choices: An untagged image layer reference no longer associated with a meaningful tag
An image stored in Docker Hub
explanation:
An untagged image layer reference no longer associated with a meaningful tag is correct because dangling images often result from rebuilds and can be cleaned up if no longer needed.

Example: intermediate build results may remain without a proper repository tag.

text: Why can container startup be fast compared with virtual machines?
choices: Containers share the host kernel instead of booting a full guest OS
explanation:
Containers share the host kernel instead of booting a full guest OS is correct because sharing the host kernel avoids the overhead of booting separate operating systems for each workload.

Example: starting a web container is often much quicker than booting a new VM image.

text: What does isolation in containers typically refer to?
choices: Separating processes, filesystems, and networking from the host and other containers
Running each app in a separate Git branch
Using only one image tag per host
explanation:
Separating processes, filesystems, and networking from the host and other containers is correct because container isolation helps applications coexist on one machine with less interference.

Example: one container cannot normally see another container’s filesystem directly.

text: What is the writable layer of a container?
choices: The temporary read-write layer added on top of the image layers at runtime
explanation:
The temporary read-write layer added on top of the image layers at runtime is correct because container writes go into a writable layer unless a volume or bind mount is used.

Example: files created during runtime disappear when the container is removed unless stored in a volume.

text: Why should databases in containers usually use volumes?
choices: Because container writable layers are ephemeral and not ideal for persistent data
Because volumes reduce CPU usage to zero
Because databases cannot use file systems otherwise
explanation:
Because container writable layers are ephemeral and not ideal for persistent data is correct because persistent storage should survive container recreation, which volumes support better than the temporary writable layer.

Example: a Postgres container should keep data in a named volume.

text: What is the purpose of docker cp?
choices: Copying files between the host and a container
Creating a new image from a container
explanation:
Copying files between the host and a container is correct because docker cp is useful for extracting logs, reports, or diagnostics without opening a shell.

Example: copy a generated report out of a batch job container.

text: What does docker commit do?
choices: Creates a new image from a container’s current filesystem state
Pushes an image to a registry
explanation:
Creates a new image from a container’s current filesystem state is correct because docker commit can snapshot a container, though reproducible Dockerfiles are usually preferred for real workflows.

Example: it may be used during ad hoc experimentation, but source-controlled builds are better long term.

text: Why is docker commit usually less preferred than editing a Dockerfile?
choices: Dockerfiles are reproducible and auditable while manual container snapshots are not
docker commit does not create images
docker commit only works on Windows
explanation:
Dockerfiles are reproducible and auditable while manual container snapshots are not is correct because infrastructure should generally be defined as code rather than remembered from interactive changes.

Example: a teammate can rebuild a Dockerfile-based image, but may not know how a committed container was modified.

text: What does docker save produce?
choices: A tar archive containing one or more images
A live backup of running container memory
explanation:
A tar archive containing one or more images is correct because docker save exports image data for transfer or backup outside a registry workflow.

Example: save an image to a tar file for an offline environment.

text: What does docker load do?
choices: Imports images from a tar archive created by docker save
Starts all containers from an image
explanation:
Imports images from a tar archive created by docker save is correct because load restores images into the local Docker image store from an exported archive.

Example: move an image into an air-gapped machine using a tar file.

text: What does docker export produce?
choices: A tar archive of a container filesystem
A full image with layer history and metadata
A running container snapshot with processes
explanation:
A tar archive of a container filesystem is correct because export flattens a container filesystem and is different from saving an image with its metadata.

Example: useful when you only need the current filesystem contents, not the image history.

text: What is the difference between docker save and docker export?
choices: save exports images with metadata and layers, while export dumps a container filesystem
export includes registry credentials and save does not
save only works for stopped containers
explanation:
save exports images with metadata and layers, while export dumps a container filesystem is correct because they target different use cases: image transport versus filesystem extraction.

Example: use save/load for moving images and export/import for raw container filesystems.

text: What does docker import create?
choices: An image from a tar archive or URL
A running container from Docker Hub
A volume from the host path
explanation:
An image from a tar archive or URL is correct because import creates a new image, often from a filesystem tarball rather than an existing layered image.

Example: import a basic root filesystem archive as a new local image.

text: What is an official image on Docker Hub?
choices: An image maintained and reviewed through Docker’s official image program
Any image with more than 100 pulls
A local image with no tag
An image built only on Windows
explanation:
An image maintained and reviewed through Docker’s official image program is correct because official images are curated and commonly used as trusted starting points for application containers.

Example: nginx and postgres official images are widely used.

text: Why should base images be chosen carefully?
choices: They affect security, size, compatibility, and update practices
They only control the container name
explanation:
They affect security, size, compatibility, and update practices is correct because a poor base image choice can make the final image larger, less secure, or harder to maintain.

Example: a slim runtime image may be preferable to a full development distribution in production.

text: What is image layering?
choices: Images are composed of stacked filesystem layers
Every container must use exactly one layer
explanation:
Images are composed of stacked filesystem layers is correct because each Dockerfile instruction can contribute a cached layer, which influences rebuild speed and image structure.

Example: changing app code may invalidate only later layers while base dependency layers remain cached.

text: Why does Docker cache layers during builds?
choices: To speed up rebuilds when earlier instructions have not changed
explanation:
To speed up rebuilds when earlier instructions have not changed is correct because build caching avoids repeating unchanged work and is one reason Dockerfile instruction order matters.

Example: install dependencies before copying frequently changing source files when appropriate.

text: Why can Dockerfile instruction order matter for performance?
choices: Because changing an earlier step can invalidate cache for later layers
Because EXPOSE must always come first
Because image tags depend on alphabetical order
explanation:
Because changing an earlier step can invalidate cache for later layers is correct because good ordering helps maximize cache reuse and reduce rebuild times.

Example: copying dependency manifests before source code can keep dependency install layers cached.

text: What is a common best practice when building application images?
choices: Use a small, explicit base image and copy only what is needed
Install every debugging tool in production by default
explanation:
Use a small, explicit base image and copy only what is needed is correct because minimal production images are easier to maintain and often safer to run.

Example: copy the built JAR into a JRE image instead of shipping the full build toolchain.

text: Why should a container usually have one main process responsibility?
choices: It keeps the container simple and aligns with Docker’s process model
Docker cannot technically run more than one process
It removes the need for logs
explanation:
It keeps the container simple and aligns with Docker’s process model is correct because single-responsibility containers are easier to observe, restart, and scale independently.

Example: run the web API in one container and the database in another.

text: Is it technically possible for a container to run multiple processes?
choices: Yes, but it is usually better to avoid unless there is a good reason
No, Docker blocks it at the kernel level
explanation:
Yes, but it is usually better to avoid unless there is a good reason is correct because containers can run multiple processes, but operational simplicity usually favors one main responsibility.

Example: use a separate sidecar or service rather than bundling unrelated daemons together.

text: What is rootless Docker?
choices: Running Docker with reduced reliance on root privileges
A way to remove all users from a container
explanation:
Running Docker with reduced reliance on root privileges is correct because rootless mode can improve security by reducing the privileges used by the Docker daemon and containers.

Example: it helps environments that want stronger isolation from root-level host access.

text: What is a common reason to use Alpine or slim base images?
choices: To reduce image size when compatible with the application needs
explanation:
To reduce image size when compatible with the application needs is correct because smaller base images can improve pull speed and reduce unnecessary packages, though compatibility should still be checked.

Example: a lightweight runtime image can be suitable for a simple API service.

text: What is Docker Desktop?
choices: A desktop application that provides Docker tools and local container support
A Kubernetes replacement for enterprises only
explanation:
A desktop application that provides Docker tools and local container support is correct because Docker Desktop packages Docker tooling, local runtime features, and optional integrations for developer machines.

Example: many macOS and Windows developers use Docker Desktop for local containers.

text: What is a common use case for Docker in development?
choices: Creating consistent local environments across team members
explanation:
Creating consistent local environments across team members is correct because Docker helps teams avoid “works on my machine” issues by standardizing runtimes and supporting services.

Example: every developer can run the same database version through a container.

text: What does docker compose up --build do?
choices: Builds images before starting Compose services
explanation:
Builds images before starting Compose services is correct because the --build flag ensures images are rebuilt if the source or Dockerfile changed before startup.

Example: useful after modifying application code and the image build definition.

text: Which command shows Docker system-wide information such as storage driver and counts?
explanation:
docker info is correct because docker info summarizes daemon configuration, storage, networking, and resource usage details.

Example: it can show how many containers and images exist locally.
